sources.title: CCRI-DRM Sub-national Tajikistan
sources.temporal_coverage: Subnational child climate and disaster risk model published July 2026; indicator vintages are not stated in the narrative PDF.
sources.methodology: UNICEF's model combines 57 indicators across hazard exposure and child vulnerability for 62 districts.
sources.limitations: Index scores compare districts within Tajikistan; the narrative does not give indicator vintages or detailed component methods.

sources.title: Climate change as a trigger of border river conflicts in Central Asia
sources.temporal_coverage: Article summarizes regional field research conducted in 2021 and a reported April 2021 border confrontation.
sources.methodology: Article summarizes field research in Sughd and regional climate-conflict dialogue.
sources.limitations: Multi-country qualitative summary; no measured climate attribution or causal estimate.

sources.title: The Nexus between Climate Change, Labour Migration, and Radicalisation among Tajik Labour Migrants
sources.organization: Royal United Services Institute and Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung Multinational Development Policy Dialogue
sources.temporal_coverage: RUSI project interviews were conducted March-May 2025; report published 28 November 2025.
sources.methodology: Qualitative scoping study with 80 interviews in Tajikistan, Turkey and remotely.
sources.limitations: Targeted sample, no survey; climate-migration attribution is uncertain and interviewees rarely cited climate directly.

sources.title: Building Resilience Across Tajikistan for a More Inclusive Economy
sources.temporal_coverage: World Bank results summary reports projects and results mainly for 2014-2023, with some operations continuing through 2027.
sources.methodology: Publisher results page summarizes several World Bank-supported programs and reported implementation outputs.
sources.limitations: Results are publisher-reported program outputs; this page does not provide an independent evaluation or isolate climate effects.

claims.locator: Pillar 1, ‘At Least Moderate Drought’, narrative p. 2.
claims.paraphrase: UNICEF rates 16 districts Very High and eight High for drought exposure; 918,108 children (26% nationally) face at least moderate drought. Temurmalik, Khuroson and Dangara are listed at 94%, 81% and 70% of their child populations, respectively.
claims.limitations: District percentages refer to the local child population; model indicator periods are not stated.

claims.paraphrase: The model reports 398,186 children (12% nationally) exposed to landslides; Rogun and Nurobod are identified as districts where children are most vulnerable, at 91% and 87% in the narrative.
claims.limitations: The narrative does not specify the denominator for the two district percentages.

claims.paraphrase: UNICEF identifies high child-service vulnerability: Nurobod and Kuhistoni Mastchoh score 10.0 for WASH vulnerability, while Vakhsh, Qubodiyon and Tojikobod face education-service delivery challenges with scores of 8.1-8.7.
claims.limitations: Scores are relative model vulnerabilities, not direct service-access rates or outcome evaluations.

claims.locator: Article sections ‘Climate change as a trigger of border river conflicts in Central Asia’ and ‘Worsening water shortages’.
claims.paraphrase: International Alert reports water-allocation disputes between Sughd and Batken preceded April 2021 armed clashes and casualties; recurring agreement breaches eroded local trust.
claims.limitations: Climate was described as a stressor, not a sole proven cause.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: International Alert links water and resource disputes to local trust loss and armed clashes, while treating climate change as a contributing stressor with understudied conflict effects.
claims.source_stated_fcv_locator: Introductory discussion of April 2021 Sughd-Batken water disputes and local trust; article paragraphs under the title.

claims.locator: Article section ‘Worsening water shortages’, paragraph on disputed infrastructure and Water User Associations.
claims.paraphrase: The source says neither state maintained disputed water infrastructure; repair attempts provoked cross-border backlash, while weak Water User Associations constrained local authorities in Sughd and Batken.
claims.limitations: The article does not evaluate a named adaptation project or quantify the capacity gap.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The source ties disputed territory to absent state maintenance and records backlash against local repairs; weak Water User Associations reduce local response capacity.
claims.source_stated_fcv_locator: ‘Worsening water shortages’, paragraph on infrastructure in disputed areas and Water User Associations.

claims.locator: Article sections ‘Regional dialogue’ and ‘About the project’.
claims.paraphrase: International Alert and ARGO convened regional climate-conflict dialogue with experts, government, local authorities and civil society, and formed a civil-society preparedness council.
claims.limitations: Dialogue outputs, not evaluated risk reductions.

claims.locator: Section 2.2, ‘How climate change impact is mediated by economic and social status’.
claims.paraphrase: RUSI interviewees described crop and livestock losses and declining farm income in Khatlon and Sughd; drought and erratic rain pressure rural livelihoods and migration decisions.
claims.limitations: Interview scoping; the source says climate interacts with poverty and unemployment, not alone.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: RUSI describes farm-climate pressure as indirectly increasing migration, mediated by poverty, unemployment and limited urban work.
claims.source_stated_fcv_locator: Section 2.2, paragraphs on Khatlon/Sughd, livelihood losses and household migration decisions, printed pp. 14-15.

claims.locator: Executive Summary and sections 3.3-3.4 on rural-origin migrants, social isolation and recruitment vulnerability, printed pp. 6 and 26-32.
claims.paraphrase: RUSI says rural-origin migrants may face culture shock, isolation and economic insecurity abroad; extremist recruiters may exploit these vulnerabilities.
claims.limitations: A possible mediated pathway, not evidence of climate-caused recruitment prevalence.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: RUSI links climate-pressured livelihoods to outmigration, then isolation and insecurity to possible recruitment vulnerability.
claims.source_stated_fcv_locator: Executive Summary findings 1-5 and sections 3.3-3.4, printed pp. 6 and 26-35.

claims.locator: Recommendations section, paragraphs on climate-resilient agriculture and the STREAM watershed programme.
claims.paraphrase: RUSI reports that the STREAM programme in the Khojibakirgan watershed reportedly shows promise: women help identify water-management gaps and shape adaptation responses.
claims.limitations: The report says the programme reportedly shows promise; it gives no measured outcome evaluation.

claims.locator: ‘Key Highlights’, bullet on the Strengthening Critical Infrastructure against Natural Hazards Project.
claims.paraphrase: The World Bank reports 17 bridges rehabilitated in GBAO, 27.5 km of embankments in Khatlon, and 20 road sections renovated, efforts benefiting 676,000 people.
institutions: Strengthening Critical Infrastructure against Natural Hazards Project
claims.limitations: Reported outputs, not measured climate-risk reduction.

claims.locator: ‘Approach’, paragraphs on the FY19-24 CPF and local resilience interventions.
claims.paraphrase: The Bank says its preventative resilience approach focused on GBAO and Khatlon, described as vulnerable to natural hazards and FCV, and included social cohesion, stronger local institutions, youth-inclusive services and livelihood support.
claims.limitations: Targeting and objectives do not show that one risk caused the other or that FCV was reduced.

claims.locator: ‘Results’, numbered item 2 on the Socio-Economic Resilience Strengthening Project.
claims.paraphrase: By 2023, SERSP reports 53 community projects and 17 youth centres completed; over 10,000 youth trained and 5,279 given livelihood support through entrepreneurship training. Women’s participation in project planning, decisions or monitoring rose from 0% to 56%.
claims.limitations: Implementation outputs and participation, not independently evaluated resilience or FCV outcomes.

search_audit.outcome: Found UNICEF’s July 2026 62-district child risk model with named district drought, landslide and service-vulnerability indicators. A 2025 World Bank poverty/climate chapter PDF was over the web reader’s size limit and not used.

search_audit.query: Tajikistan climate change conflict security farmer herder GBAO climate conflict mediator primary report 2024 2025
search_audit.outcome: Found International Alert’s analysis of water-allocation disputes and border tensions around Sughd-Batken, and RUSI’s qualitative climate-livelihood-migration-radicalisation pathway. Both sources describe multiple mediators and attribution limits.

search_audit.query: Tajikistan climate hazards violence insecurity adaptation access project local 2024 2025 report
search_audit.outcome: International Alert reports disputed infrastructure, cross-border backlash to community repairs and weak Water User Associations that constrained local response; no inspected source establishes armed violence blocking a named climate-adaptation operation.

search_audit.query: Tajikistan community climate adaptation resilience outcomes 2024 2025 UN World Bank report Sughd Khatlon GBAO
search_audit.outcome: Found RUSI’s discussion of women’s participation in the Khojibakirgan STREAM adaptation programme and World Bank-reported disaster infrastructure and community-resilience outputs in GBAO/Khatlon; the sources do not provide independent impact evaluation.

gaps: UNICEF's district model is a relative index; indicator dates and detailed methods are not specified in its narrative PDF.

The 2021 International Alert report identifies climate and resource pressures as contributors to border tension but does not establish climate as a sole cause of armed clashes; exact affected groups and local causal pathways remain contested.

No inspected source documents armed violence directly preventing a named climate adaptation project in Tajikistan; the observed reverse-direction evidence concerns disputed water infrastructure and local resource-management capacity.

RUSI's climate-migration-radicalisation chain is qualitative and indirect. The report notes migration is driven primarily by economic/social factors, most migrant interviewees did not identify climate change directly, and the proposed recruitment pathway is not a prevalence estimate.
World Bank sources describe reported outputs and an FCV-sensitive multi-risk program in GBAO/Khatlon, not measured climate-attributable resilience or a causal climate-FCV effect.
The World Bank poverty/climate chapter exceeded the web reader's content-size limit; the GCF and ADB pages returned 403, so no findings from those sources were used.
